questions.q: What distinction does the author make between a hazardous asteroid and a near-Earth asteroid?
choices: Near-Earth objects are defined by their brightness rather than their paths.
Only objects larger than Dimorphos can be classified as near-Earth.
Orbital proximity is a category of position, not proof of impact danger.
A hazardous asteroid must already be moving unpredictably.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 1 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why can an apparently alarming rise in impact probability still be consistent with better science?
choices: The object's physical orbit necessarily changes with each announcement.
The range of possible trajectories is changing as fresh evidence narrows it.
An increase shows that astronomers have abandoned mathematical modelling.
Every later estimate must be higher until the object is visible.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: How do infrared observations complement ordinary optical searches?
choices: They provide complete knowledge of all objects in the solar system.
They eliminate the need to compare images taken on different nights.
They change a faint asteroid into a brighter object.
They may reveal thermal emissions from bodies difficult to see in reflected light.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: What does the DART experiment leave uncertain about a future response to a different asteroid?
choices: A successful strike does not specify the deflection produced by another target's structure.
It is not known whether the spacecraft reached Dimorphos at all.
The test was carried out after a real impact had already occurred.
The mission proved that warning time is irrelevant to any response.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why did debris ejected by the DART collision matter?
choices: It stopped astronomers from making any further measurements.
It proved that Dimorphos was an entirely solid boulder.
It contributed to the change in orbit beyond the spacecraft's own momentum.
It caused the asteroid to leave the solar system.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why was the follow-up Hera mission scientifically useful?
choices: It could investigate the target's material and the details of the measured response.
It was intended to repeat the same collision immediately.
It would remove the need for any future telescope surveys.
It was needed to give Dimorphos a new name.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why may a small deflection made years before a possible impact be more useful than a dramatic last-minute action?
choices: Asteroids are easier to see only after they have passed Earth.
A small early change can grow into a useful separation over time.
A last-minute spacecraft would always miss the asteroid.
An early warning automatically changes the asteroid's orbit.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: A news report publishes a risk percentage but omits the date of the estimate. What is the key problem?
choices: The article must use a more frightening photograph to gain attention.
Risk percentages are meaningless in all circumstances.
The date alone determines whether the object is dangerous.
Readers cannot assess the changing evidence and the estimate's uncertainty.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 5 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why does the writer treat coordinated surveys and public explanations as part of planetary defence?
choices: They are useful only after a deflection spacecraft has been launched.
They make proportionate decisions possible before a physical response is considered.
Their main purpose is to reduce public interest in science.
They guarantee that future estimates will never change.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 5 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Which communication policy is closest to the author's ideal?
choices: Report only the highest risk estimate to avoid confusing the audience.
Avoid all discussion until every possible trajectory is excluded.
Describe every close approach as an emergency to attract resources.
Explain revisions openly while acknowledging both uncertainty and the value of preparation.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 5 of the original C1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.
